analysis.one_liner: Taxes private equity and hedge fund managers' carried-interest pay as regular income instead of at lower capital gains rates.
analysis.headline: The bill to tax carried interest as ordinary income was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee in March 2019 and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: When a private equity or hedge fund manager takes a share of the fund's profits as pay, current law taxes that money at the lower long-term capital gains rate instead of the higher rates that apply to wages and salaries. This bill would have ended that treatment: a manager's profits share would be taxed as ordinary income, would count toward self-employment taxes, and underpayments from avoiding the rule would carry a doubled penalty. The bill never advanced past its referral to the tax-writing committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Federal taxpayers broadly, who currently make up for the tax revenue forgone when fund managers' labor income is taxed at investment rates; the bill would also modestly level the playing field between finance professionals and wage earners who cannot recharacterize their salaries as capital gains.

how_it_helps.text: It taxes the profits share (carried interest) earned by private equity, hedge fund, and real estate managers as ordinary income rather than at the lower long-term capital gains rate, closing a gap under which compensation for managing other people's money is taxed like an investment.

It subjects that income to self-employment taxes, which currently do not apply to it, and doubles the accuracy-related penalty to 40% for underpayments from avoiding the new rules, strengthening enforcement.

analysis.who_pays: Private equity, hedge fund, and real estate investment managers, whose share of fund profits would be taxed at ordinary income rates up to 37% plus self-employment taxes instead of the 20% capital gains rate.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private equity and hedge fund managers

drawbacks.text: Critics of ending carried interest treatment argue it raises taxes on fund managers' compensation and could reduce incentives for investment in private equity and venture capital, which finance startups and business turnarounds.

The bill's rules are highly complex, including detailed valuation, tiered-partnership, and anti-abuse provisions, which would create compliance costs and disputes over how the rules apply — a burden supporters would have to defend against a simpler rate-based approach.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is a fairer tax structure — fund managers' performance pay would be taxed like other work income rather than like long-term investment gains — with revenue accruing to the Treasury. The drawbacks are that it raises the tax burden on a specific set of professionals without directly lowering anyone else's taxes, and its complexity invites aggressive structuring; however, its anti-abuse provisions and doubled penalty show the drafters anticipated that. The larger honest cost is that it was never seriously considered: it died without debate, so the drawbacks and benefits were never tested on the merits.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee, whose chair never scheduled it for consideration, so it sat there until the two-year Congress ended without a vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 13, 2019 and referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, the committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation.
That is the only action ever taken: the record shows no hearing, no committee markup, no vote, and no floor consideration before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

The bill would have rewritten the tax code so that fund managers' investment-services partnership income is treated as ordinary income, and it would have repealed the section 1061 carried interest provision enacted in 2017.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fund managers who collect carried interest kept the lower capital-gains tax rate on their compensation, and the broader tax code was left unchanged. Ordinary taxpayers gained nothing from a bill that would have shifted tax toward high-earning finance professionals.

for.name: Rep. Bill Pascrell Jr.
for.role: Sponsor, House Ways and Means Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 18 original cosponsors, including Ways and Means members.

for.name: 37 of 231 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all cosponsors were Democrats and no Republican signed on.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the remainder of the Congress.

against.name: Private equity and hedge fund industry
against.role: Private equity, hedge fund, and venture capital lobby
against.what_they_did: Long opposed changes to carried interest taxation; well-documented lobbying in Washington has repeatedly stalled such proposals, including the 2017 effort that produced only the section 1061 holding-period tweak this bill would have repealed.

sides.party_line_note: All 37 cosponsors were House Democrats and no Republican supported the bill, which died in a committee controlled by the Democratic majority without ever reaching the floor.

industries.industry: Private equity, hedge fund, and real estate fund managers
industries.note: Their carried interest would be taxed at ordinary income rates up to 37% instead of the 20% long-term capital gains rate, plus self-employment tax, with a 40% penalty for avoidance. Fund managers are among the highest-paid people in finance, and this treatment has saved them billions over time.

Funds themselves would face new compliance and recordkeeping requirements and some restructuring of manager compensation, though the bill exempts genuine capital invested by partners and family partnerships, so investors' own capital gains remain untouched.
